title: Playing waltz tunes then breaking into fox-trot
summary: Joe explains that bands would play a tune like I Wonder What's Become of Sally as a waltz and then pick it up in double time, which dancers loved.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Now, there's a thing I wanted to ask you about. A lot of the old New Orleans bands would do that, play it as a waltz, then end it, then pick it up in, you know, like fox-trot time or anything like that. Was that just for the dances, or was that because you liked to put Jazz in there? Or was it?

That was just because we liked to play it that way. And the (?) would just fall right in there and start dancing. But usually... I don't remember... We would play it in the waltz and finish it, flat out, and then people would applaud, CLAP-CLAP, and then we'd go into a
Yeah, that seems to be it. But I've never been able to pin that down, whether it was because the dancers wanted the foxtrot, or just because the band...
No, the dancers... As I remember it, when we started doing it, it was kind of new to us and new to the dancers, too. And they just loved it.

Funny that you mentioned that particular piece. I recorded that in 1966 as a waltz with Percy Humphrey and Louis Nelson and Albert Beauvais(?). And at the end of the waltz, Percy just automatically, up, bop, and away they went in regular 4/4 cut time, straight away, without... It just came so natural to him to do that. After he got through playing a waltz, he just went straight into the Jazz part of it, you know. I guess that was a throwback from the old days that you're talking about.

Well, the thing about it, we started doing this as kids... These guys were far more advanced than we was, you see. But after I was grown up, though, like with the Martel Band, that was a common thing, because... Now, that was a pretty good band.
